seed.topic: Explore the prime-generating polynomial n^2 + n + 41

explorer.title: Euler’s Prime-Generating Polynomial
explorer.object_definition: Define P(n) = n^2 + n + 41 for every nonnegative integer n.
observations: The exact values P(0) through P(10) are 41, 43, 47, 53, 61, 71, 83, 97, 113, 131, and 151.
Wolfram’s exact PrimeQ test returned True for every P(n) from n = 0 through n = 39.
No case at n = 40 or beyond was tested.
This finite evidence is compelling but does not prove a universal statement.
explorer.conjecture: P(n) is prime for every nonnegative integer n.
explorer.plain_english_summary: This simple number-making rule produces a prime for each of its first forty inputs. The tempting conjecture is that it will keep producing primes forever.
explorer.why_it_looks_true: The conjecture survives 40 consecutive initial cases. Throughout the tested interval, the polynomial grows from 41 to 1601 without producing a single composite value, making the universal pattern look unusually persuasive.

wolfram_evidence.expression: With[{P = Function[{n}, n^2 + n + 41]}, Table[{n, P[n]}, {n, 0, 10}]]
wolfram_evidence.interpretation: This generates exact initial values of P(n).

wolfram_evidence.expression: With[{P = Function[{n}, n^2 + n + 41]}, Table[{n, P[n], PrimeQ[P[n]]}, {n, 0, 39}]]
wolfram_evidence.interpretation: Every one of the 40 permitted initial cases is reported prime.

falsifier.search_strategy: Used the exact predicate !PrimeQ[n^2+n+41] over Range[0,5000] in ascending order and selected the first match. Independently confirmed its factorization and confirmed every preceding case n=0 through 39 is prime.
falsifier.counterexample_explanation: At n=40, P(40)=40^2+40+41=1681=41×41, so it is composite. Every admissible n below 40 passes PrimeQ, making n=40 the smallest counterexample.

wolfram_checks.expression: FirstCase[Range[0, 5000], n_ /; ! PrimeQ[n^2 + n + 41] :> {n, n^2 + n + 41}, Missing["NotFound"]]
wolfram_checks.interpretation: The exact ascending search finds n=40 as the first composite-producing input.
1681 has prime factorization 41^2, direct substitution confirms the equality, and every preceding value from n=0 through 39 is prime.

prover.repaired_conjecture: Let P(n)=n^2+n+41 for nonnegative integers n. Then P(n) is prime for every 0 <= n <= 39. Furthermore, 41 divides P(n) if and only if n is congruent to 0 or -1 modulo 41. Consequently, every positive n in either of those two residue classes produces a composite value; explicitly, for every integer k >= 1, P(41 k)=41 (41 k^2+k+1) and P(41 k-1)=41 (41 k^2-k+1).
prover.repair_type: Falsified universal claim replaced by an exact finite prime range and an infinite structural family of composite values.
proof_outline: The original conjecture fails first at n=40: P(40)=1681=41^2.
Exact primality testing certifies every value P(n) for 0 <= n <= 39. This proves the stated finite-range claim; it is not treated as evidence for an unrestricted claim.
Modulo 41, P(n) is congruent to n(n+1). Since 41 is prime, this vanishes exactly when n is congruent to 0 or -1 modulo 41.
Substitution gives P(41k)=41(41k^2+k+1) and P(41k-1)=41(41k^2-k+1). For k >= 1, each cofactor is greater than 1, so these values are composite.
Thus the repaired statement supplies infinitely many counterexamples while retaining the exact exceptional initial run of 40 primes.
prover.certificate_expression: {And @@ Table[PrimeQ[n^2 + n + 41], {n, 0, 39}], Resolve[ForAll[n, Equivalent[Mod[n^2 + n + 41, 41] == 0, Mod[n, 41] == 0 || Mod[n, 41] == 40]], Integers], FullSimplify[{(41 k)^2 + 41 k + 41 == 41 (41 k^2 + k + 1), (41 k - 1)^2 + (41 k - 1) + 41 == 41 (41 k^2 - k + 1)}, Element[k, Integers]], FactorInteger[40^2 + 40 + 41]}
discoveries: The prime-generating run is exactly certified through n=39, and the next input already fails.
The two residue classes n congruent to 0 and -1 modulo 41 contain infinitely many composite-producing inputs.
The qualification 'positive' is necessary for the class n congruent to 0 modulo 41, because n=0 gives the prime value 41.
No assertion is made that every input n >= 40 produces a composite value.

wolfram_checks.interpretation: Symbolically verifies both parametrized factorizations for every integer k.

wolfram_checks.expression: {And @@ Table[PrimeQ[n^2 + n + 41], {n, 0, 39}], 40^2 + 40 + 41, FactorInteger[40^2 + 40 + 41], And @@ Table[! PrimeQ[n^2 + n + 41], {n, Join[Range[40, 410, 41], Range[41, 410, 41]]}]}
wolfram_checks.interpretation: Independently checks the precise initial prime range, the first counterexample and its factorization, and sample members of both infinite residue families.
Certifies the exact residue-class characterization of divisibility by 41 for all integers n.

certificate.expression: {And @@ Table[PrimeQ[n^2 + n + 41], {n, 0, 39}], Resolve[ForAll[n, Equivalent[Mod[n^2 + n + 41, 41] == 0, Mod[n, 41] == 0 || Mod[n, 41] == 40]], Integers], FullSimplify[{(41 k)^2 + 41 k + 41 == 41 (41 k^2 + k + 1), (41 k - 1)^2 + (41 k - 1) + 41 == 41 (41 k^2 - k + 1)}, Element[k, Integers]], FactorInteger[40^2 + 40 + 41]}
